models.name: Model G
models.summary: Introduced in 1936 in "monofilm" and "multifilm" models; the multifilm included a tool-free parts kit of reel spindles, sprockets, gate and guide-rollers to adapt the projector to various film gauges.
Projected 8mm film at fixed speeds of 18 and 5 frames per second forward, and 18 fps in reverse.

models.name: M-8

models.name: SM 8
models.summary: Magnetic sound projection and recording, with a built-in 2W / 15 Ohm speaker.

models.name: S-221
models.summary: Plays back silent or sound film with optical or magnetic tracks, and records sound onto 16mm magnetic-striped film.

models.name: SM 80 Programmatic
models.summary: The top of Bolex's Super 8 sound range at the end of the 1970s, and a different machine from the SP 80 despite the name. It records on both sound tracks rather than one, takes 800ft reels rather than 600, and carries a Bolex Hi-Fi f/1.2 12.5 to 25mm zoom and a 100W halogen lamp with a dichroic reflector. A track selector gives either track or both, with fading, sound-on-sound, an automatic level limiter, manual override and an LED meter; a sync socket also drives an outside tape recorder, so it works single or double system. 18 and 24 frames a second, with a counter. Built in Austria by Eumig. Bolex (U.S.A.) listed it at $780.00 in April 1979, the dearest projector on the page.

sources.title: Bolex Super 8 Cameras and Projectors, price list no. S1, 1 April 1979
sources.note: Bolex (U.S.A.) Inc.'s own list: "Bolex SM-80 Programmatic", product 93480, $780.00 suggested retail. Read off the rendered page, which matters here: the scan's text layer runs the neighbouring rows' model numbers into their lens specifications and invents models that do not exist. The list hyphenates the name; this entry does not, to match the SM 8 and SP 80 beside it.

sources.title: Super8Data, Bolex SM 80 Programmatic
sources.note: A collector database, so secondary. Everything above except the price comes from it, and it is also what settles the machine's identity: it dates the SM 80 Programmatic to 1977 with a 240m reel, recording on both tracks and a f/1.2 12.5 to 25mm lens, against the SP 80's 1973 to 1974 run, 180m reel and single track. The two are not the same projector under two names, which is the easy mistake to make from the price list alone.

models.name: SP 8
models.summary: A Super 8 magnetic sound projector that records as well as plays back, sold from 1972 with a f/1.3 15 to 30mm zoom, a 100W 12V lamp, automatic threading, forward and reverse running, 18 and 24 frames a second and 600ft reels. Sound goes on the main track, with fading and sound-on-sound, and the level can be set by hand or left to an automatic limiter. Built in Austria by Eumig, who had bought Bolex in 1969, on the same chassis as Eumig's own Mark S. Paillard's February 1972 dealer list prices it at $299.50, between the 18-5L Super at $199.50 and the SM8 Sound at $449.50. A SP 8 Special was also sold, and the later SP 80 is built on it: Bolex's booklet covering both Specials calls them practically identical, the SP 8 special's amplifier being the smaller at 6W sinusoidal against 10W.

sources.title: Bolex Super 8mm Confidential Price List, 23 February 1972
sources.note: The primary source, and the reason this entry exists. Paillard's own dealer list: "SP8 SOUND, product 2480, w/f/1.3 15-30mm Zoom Lens", $299.50 suggested retail. Read off the rendered page. Scanned by Pacific Rim Camera.

sources.title: Bolex SP 80 special and SP 8 special, instruction booklet
sources.note: A Bolex document for this family at last, where this file long said one was wanted. It covers the two Special variants together and opens by saying they are "practically identical, except for a few details", which is Bolex settling in its own words that the SP 8 and SP 80 are one design. One of the few details is power: the booklet gives the SP 80 special 10W sinusoidal and 15W musical against the SP 8 special's 6W and 8W. Both are supplied with a Bolex Hi-Fi zoom, a 12V 100W halogen lamp with a dichroic mirror and a 400ft reel, and both are for silent and magnetic sound Super 8. Response 75 to 10,000 cycles at 18 f.p.s., signal to noise 45dB, wow under 0.4 per cent, footage counter reading one unit to 18 frames. It describes the Special variants rather than the plain models, so it is evidence about the family and not a datasheet for either base machine. Scanned by Pacific Rim Camera.

sources.title: Super8Data, Bolex SP 8
sources.note: A collector database, so secondary, but it dates the machine to 1972 and gives the same f/1.3 15 to 30mm lens the price list does, which is the two sources agreeing without having seen each other. Everything above beyond the price and the lens comes from here: the lamp, the reel size, the speeds, the sound arrangement and the Eumig Mark S chassis. The specifications it gives beyond that, down to the amplifier's transistor count, have not been repeated here because none of them has been checked against a Bolex document.

models.name: SP 80
models.summary: A Super 8 and Single-8 projector with magnetic sound it can both record and play back, with automatic threading, forward and reverse running, 18 and 24 frames a second and 600ft reels. From after Eumig acquired Bolex in 1969, and built on Eumig's own mechanism rather than a Sainte-Croix design. A variant was sold as the SP 80 Special, and Bolex's own booklet for it says the SP 80 special and SP 8 special are practically identical, differing mainly in amplifier power: 10W sinusoidal against the SP 8 special's 6W.

sources.title: Dealer and collector listings, read November 2026
sources.note: Everything above comes from people selling or restoring the machine, not from Paillard or Eumig. They agree on the format, the sound, the speeds and the reel size, and date it to 1973 to 1975. They disagree on which Eumig chassis underlies it, the 700 or the 800 series, so this entry does not say. A Bolex booklet for the Special variants has since been read and is cited above; it does not date the machine or settle the chassis question, so those still rest on the listings.

models.name: 18-9 DUO
models.summary: The projector that takes everything. Reels from 50 to 400 feet, Kodak cartridges from 50 to 400 feet, and regular 8 as well as Super 8, which is what the DUO means. 18 frames a second or 9 for slow motion. A f/1.3 15-30mm Paillard Bolex Hi-Fi zoom and a 100W mirror halogen lamp. It stops itself at the end of the film, the film can stay attached to the reel so nothing needs fixing on before a rewind, and it rewinds fast through the gate or reel to reel, whether the film ran all the way through or not. $189.50 in February 1972.

models.summary: A 16mm sound projector that records as well as plays, and the most serious projector Bolex made. It takes any 16mm film, single or double perforated, silent or with an optical or a magnetic track, and will record on the magnetic stripe with direct mixing, superimposition and sound fading. Spools to 2000ft, automatic threading, a low-voltage motor under electronic regulation, and speeds of 18 and 24 with anything from 12 to 26 on a potentiometer, plus freezing on a frame and single-frame projection. The amplifier is fully transistorised in three plug-in units, 25W at 2 per cent distortion into 8 ohms, with a 3W monitor speaker in the body and a 10W one in the lid. Recording level is set on separate microphone and phono potentiometers and watched on a lit VU meter, with threshold compression, a variable-erasure control for dissolves, and a double lock so nothing is erased by accident. Magnetic response 100 to 12,000 cycles at 24 f.p.s., optical 50 to 7,000, wow under 0.3 per cent. A 24V 250W halogen lamp with a dichroic mirror and a choice of three lenses, 50mm f/1.3, 70mm f/1.6 or the 35-65mm f/1.6 zoom. Die-cast aluminium with a plastic lid that forms its case, 480 by 380 by 240mm, about 40lb. $3,727.00 in January 1978.

models.summary: A 16mm projector for silent films and for sound films with either an optical or a magnetic track, which is the 521's range of playback without its recording. Bolex sold it on its speeds: several of them, with freezing on a frame and single-frame projection, which the brochure recommends to schools because movement can be taken apart and looked at phase by phase. Universal model for 118 to 240V at 50 or 60Hz, with the Kiptaron 50mm f/1.3 or the Bolex Hi-Fi 35-65mm f/1.6 zoom.

models.summary: The plainest of the three, and sold as such: a 16mm projector for silent films and for sound films with an optical track only, meant for showing hired prints rather than making anything. Bolex's own pitch is ease of use and an attractive price, and its reasoning is that almost every hired film carries an optical track, the exceptions being originals and films that exist in only a few copies. Universal model for 118 to 240V at 50 or 60Hz, with the Kiptaron 50mm f/1.3 or the Bolex Hi-Fi 35-65mm f/1.6 zoom.
